nodes.name: Aftermath
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: The assassination led directly to World War I through a complex web of alliances and diplomatic failures. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, issued an ultimatum to Serbia. When Serbia's response was deemed insufficient, Austria-Hungary declared war on July 28, 1914, exactly one month after the assassination.

nodes.name: AustriaDeclaresWar
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: On July 28, 1914, exactly one month after the assassination, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. This activated a chain of alliance commitments: Russia mobilized to support Serbia, Germany declared war on Russia, France entered to support Russia, and Germany invaded Belgium, bringing Britain into the war.

nodes.name: BlackHand
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Officially known as "Unification or Death," the Black Hand was a secret Serbian nationalist society formed in 1901. Led by Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević (known as Apis), it aimed to unite all South Slavic territories. The organization provided weapons, training, and support to the assassins.

nodes.name: FatalShot
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Gavrilo Princip fired two shots. The first hit Sophie in the abdomen, and the second struck Franz Ferdinand in the neck, severing his jugular vein. Sophie died almost immediately, while Franz Ferdinand died about 10 minutes later. His last words were reportedly "Sophie, Sophie, don't die. Stay alive for the children."

nodes.name: FranzFerdinand
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Archduke Franz Ferdinand (1863-1914) was the heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne. His assassination sparked a chain of events leading to WWI. He was known for his support of federalism and greater autonomy for ethnic groups within the empire, which made him controversial among Serbian nationalists.

nodes.name: GavriloPrincip
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Gavrilo Princip (1894-1918) was a Bosnian Serb nationalist who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie. A member of Young Bosnia and backed by the Black Hand, he was 19 years old at the time. He was too young for the death penalty and received a 20-year sentence, dying of tuberculosis in prison in 1918.

nodes.name: JulyUltimatum
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: On July 23, 1914, Austria-Hungary delivered a 10-point ultimatum to Serbia with a 48-hour deadline. The demands were intentionally harsh and designed to be unacceptable, including allowing Austro-Hungarian officials to participate in the investigation on Serbian soil. Serbia accepted most points but rejected those violating its sovereignty.

nodes.name: LatinBridge
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Latin Bridge (Latinska ćuprija) is an Ottoman-era bridge over the Miljacka River in Sarajevo. It was the location where Gavrilo Princip shot Franz Ferdinand and Sophie. The spot is now marked with a memorial plaque and is a significant historical site.

nodes.name: Sarajevo
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Capital and largest city of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1914, it was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. The city had significant ethnic tensions between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. The assassination occurred during the Archduke's visit to inspect military maneuvers.

nodes.name: SarajevoAssassination
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914. This event is widely considered the trigger that set off World War I. The attack was carried out by Gavrilo Princip, a member of the Young Bosnia movement, backed by the Serbian secret society Black Hand.

nodes.name: SophieChotek
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg (1868-1914), wife of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. She was killed alongside her husband in the Sarajevo assassination. Her marriage to Franz Ferdinand was considered morganatic, and she faced significant social restrictions at the imperial court.

nodes.name: Timeline-Attempt1
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: June 28, 1914, 10:15 AM - The first assassination attempt by Nedeljko Čabrinović, who threw a bomb at the Archduke's car. The bomb bounced off and exploded under the next car, injuring several people. Čabrinović attempted suicide by jumping into the river but was captured.

nodes.name: Timeline-CityHall
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: June 28, 1914, 10:45 AM - After the bomb attempt, the motorcade proceeded to City Hall where Franz Ferdinand gave a speech. He was visibly angry about the attack. A decision was made to change the route to visit the wounded at the hospital.

nodes.name: Timeline-FatalMoment
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: June 28, 1914, 11:15 AM - At Latin Bridge, the driver took a wrong turn. While reversing, the car stalled directly in front of Gavrilo Princip, who fired two shots from about 5 feet away. Both Franz Ferdinand and Sophie were fatally wounded.

nodes.name: Timeline-Morning
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: June 28, 1914, 10:00 AM - The Archduke and Sophie arrived at Sarajevo railway station. The date was particularly provocative as it was St. Vitus' Day (Vidovdan), a Serbian national holiday commemorating the Battle of Kosovo.

nodes.name: Trial
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: The trial of the conspirators began on October 12, 1914, in Sarajevo. Twenty-five defendants were charged. The proceedings were conducted in German, which many defendants didn't speak well. The trial was widely criticized as being politically motivated rather than seeking true justice.

nodes.name: Verdict
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Gavrilo Princip was found guilty on October 28, 1914. Because he was under 20 years old at the time of the assassination, he could not be sentenced to death under Austro-Hungarian law. He received the maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. Three other conspirators received death sentences and were executed.

nodes.name: Weapon
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: Browning M1910 semi-automatic pistol, serial number M19074, caliber .380 ACP (9×17mm). The weapon was provided by the Black Hand organization. After the assassination, it became key evidence and is now displayed in the Museum of Military History in Vienna.

nodes.name: WWI
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: World War I (1914-1918) resulted in over 16 million deaths and 21 million wounded. It ended with the collapse of four empires: Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, Russian, and German. The Treaty of Versailles and other peace settlements reshaped Europe's political map and set the stage for WWII.

nodes.name: YoungBosnia
nodes.author: ANDREW
nodes.notes: A revolutionary movement of predominantly Serb, but also Croat and Muslim South Slav students in Austria-Hungary who wanted to break away from the empire. Members were influenced by anarchist and nationalist ideologies. Gavrilo Princip was a key member.
